context_blurb:
The periodic table lines up the elements by the protons in each atom's nucleus, in rows called periods, so that elements that behave alike share a column, or group. It explains why one metal fizzes in water and another explodes, and it let chemists foretell unseen elements.

An atom's electrons sit in shells around the nucleus, and the outer shell decides how it reacts. Neon's ten electrons fill shells of two and eight, so its outer shell is full, with nothing to gain or lose. Fluorine (two and seven) is one electron short and sodium (two, eight, one) has one to spare, so both react fiercely.

A column's elements share their number of outer electrons, so they act alike. The first column's alkali metals each have one outer electron and react by giving it up. Each step down the column adds a shell, so the outer electron sits farther out, screened from the nucleus by more inner electrons, and comes away more easily. So lithium only fizzes in water; caesium explodes.

The halogens, fluorine down to iodine, run the other way, growing less reactive down the column: each has seven outer electrons and takes in one more. Fluorine's outer shell lies closest to its nucleus, with the fewest inner electrons in the way, so its small atom pulls hardest on an electron it takes in. Iodine has more protons, 53 to fluorine's 9, but its outer shell lies much farther out.

Across a row, from sodium to chlorine, every new electron goes into the same third shell while the inner shells stay put. So more protons pull harder on the same outer shell, and the atoms shrink, chlorine's to about half sodium's width, even as they grow heavier.

In 1869 Dmitri Mendeleev ordered the known elements by atomic weight, how heavy their atoms are, leaving gaps where nothing fitted. Below aluminium he forecast a low-melting metal weighing about 68, and in 1875 Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran discovered gallium, weighing 69.7 and melting below 30 degrees Celsius. Lecoq de Boisbaudran's first density, 4.7, was off; Mendeleev had written that it would be 5.9, and purer metal gave 5.9. A table built to fit the known elements was bound to fit them; a forecast made before the metal was found could fail, and did not.

Eka means one place below. Mendeleev's eka-silicon had to fall between silicon above it and tin below it in the same column, so with no sample to weigh he read its weight, about 72, off the trend down that column. Silicon itself weighs only about 28. In 1886 Clemens Winkler found it, germanium, at 72.6, the best confirmation of the table up to then.

Mendeleev trusted chemistry over weight. Tellurium is slightly heavier than iodine, yet iodine acts like chlorine and bromine, so Mendeleev put it with them, after tellurium, and claimed tellurium had been weighed wrongly. Brauner's 1883 weighing gave about 125, and Mendeleev cited it, but later careful weighings showed tellurium (127.6) really is heavier than iodine (126.9).

In 1913 Henry Moseley struck metals with electrons and found that each metal's X-rays rose in frequency by one even step per element. Each step is one more proton in the nucleus. Cobalt, though a little heavier, sits one step before nickel because it has one proton fewer, 27 against nickel's 28. The table is a count of protons, the atomic number, not an order of weights. Though Moseley never measured tellurium or iodine, the same count, 52 protons against 53, puts tellurium first.

The rare-earth metals, lanthanum to lutetium, are so alike that chemists of the early 1900s sometimes mistook a blend of two for one pure metal. Because each element's X-rays rise one even step above the last's, every element takes one whole number, none skipped and none spare, so there was room for exactly fifteen, lanthanum and lutetium included. A sniper killed Moseley at Gallipoli in 1915, aged 27.

Lord Rayleigh noticed that nitrogen drawn from air was heavier, litre for litre, by about half a percent, than nitrogen made from chemicals. William Ramsay soaked up air's nitrogen with hot magnesium until a trace of gas remained that would react with nothing. They named it argon in 1894, from a Greek word meaning lazy, and its weight, about 40, matched no empty square. Argon proved the first of a whole family the table lacked: neon, krypton and xenon followed in 1898, and in 1902 Mendeleev gave them a column.
